title: Life during the Second World War
description: The Home Front, rationing, civilian opposition, the Final Solution and the impact of defeat in 1945.
hero_keywords: German civilians World War Two home front rubble
content_html:
The German Home Front in the Early War Years

Germany went to war in September 1939 with an economy that had not fully converted to a wartime footing. In the early years of the war, as German forces won rapid victories across Europe, the regime tried to shield the German civilian population from significant sacrifice. Consumer goods remained available longer than in other belligerent nations, and rationing — though introduced — was less severe than in Britain during the same period. The regime feared that excessive hardship would undermine popular support, having studied how the Home Front had collapsed in 1918.

Joseph Goebbels managed information carefully, ensuring early German victories were celebrated while setbacks were minimised or explained away. Radio broadcasts, cinema newsreels and newspapers all presented a filtered picture of the war.

Key Fact

After the German defeat at Stalingrad in early 1943, Goebbels declared 'total war' in a speech at the Berlin Sportpalast on 18 February 1943. This meant the full mobilisation of the German economy and society for the war effort — longer working hours, more women in factories, and severe reductions in consumer goods.

Total War: Changing Conditions from 1943

The turning point came with the German surrender at Stalingrad in February 1943. Approximately 300,000 German and Axis soldiers had been encircled; roughly 91,000 surrendered, including Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus. The defeat shattered the myth of German invincibility and marked the beginning of a strategic retreat on the Eastern Front. Goebbels responded by mobilising public sentiment, calling for sacrifice in his 'total war' speech.

From 1943, conditions on the German Home Front deteriorated sharply. Albert Speer, as Armaments Minister, reorganised industrial production to maximise military output. Women were increasingly drafted into factory work despite the earlier ideology that women belonged in the home. Food and goods rationing tightened. By 1944–1945, Allied bombing campaigns — both British night bombing and American daylight precision raids — were causing massive civilian casualties and destroying industrial capacity in German cities.

Allied bombing caused enormous destruction in German cities. The firebombing of Hamburg in July–August 1943 (Operation Gomorrah) killed an estimated 37,000 people and left approximately one million homeless. Dresden was firebombed in February 1945 with heavy civilian casualties, though exact figures remain disputed by historians. The bombing disrupted industrial production, forced the dispersal of factories and consumed massive German anti-aircraft resources — diverting weapons and personnel from the front.

Opposition to the Nazis During the War

Organised opposition to the Nazi regime was extremely dangerous, but it existed. The White Rose was a small student resistance group at Munich University. Hans and Sophie Scholl and their associates distributed leaflets calling for passive resistance against Hitler's regime. They were arrested in February 1943, tried before the People's Court, and executed by guillotine. Their moral courage became a symbol of principled opposition to Nazism.

The most significant act of resistance came from within the military. On 20 July 1944, Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg placed a bomb at Hitler's military headquarters at Rastenburg — the July Plot. Hitler survived because the briefcase containing the bomb was moved behind a heavy table leg. Approximately 7,000 people were arrested in the subsequent purge; around 4,980 were executed, including Stauffenberg. The plot's failure strengthened Hitler's belief in his destiny and led to even more brutal repression.

Key Fact

The White Rose distributed anti-Nazi leaflets in 1942–43; its leaders, Hans and Sophie Scholl, were executed in February 1943. The July Plot (1944) was a military attempt to assassinate Hitler; it failed and approximately 7,000 were arrested and around 4,980 were executed in reprisals.

The Final Solution

The persecution of Jews escalated dramatically once the war began. In territories conquered by Germany — Poland, the Soviet Union and beyond — mobile killing units called Einsatzgruppen shot hundreds of thousands of Jews, Roma, Soviet officials and others in mass killings. The scale of murder by shooting was enormous — at Babi Yar near Kyiv in September 1941, approximately 33,771 Jews were killed over two days.

At the Wannsee Conference on 20 January 1942, senior Nazi officials coordinated the bureaucratic machinery for the systematic murder of all European Jews, a programme they termed the 'Final Solution to the Jewish Question'. Death camps were established at Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec, Chelmno and Majdanek in occupied Poland. These were industrialised killing centres equipped with gas chambers. The majority of victims were murdered in gas chambers using Zyklon B at Auschwitz or carbon monoxide at the other camps. Historians estimate that approximately six million Jewish people were murdered in the Holocaust between 1941 and 1945.

By early 1945 the Soviet Red Army was advancing rapidly from the east and Allied forces from the west. Germany's cities lay in ruins from bombing; millions were displaced. Hitler retreated to a bunker beneath the Berlin Reich Chancellery. On 30 April 1945 he died by suicide as Soviet forces entered the city. Germany surrendered unconditionally on 8 May 1945 — known as VE Day (Victory in Europe Day). The war had killed an estimated 5–7 million German civilians and soldiers. Germany lay physically destroyed and morally discredited, its infrastructure shattered, its government abolished and its territory about to be divided among the victorious powers.
exam_tip_html: For questions about the Final Solution, handle with precision: name the Wannsee Conference (January 1942), the Einsatzgruppen killings in the Soviet Union from 1941, and the death camps in occupied Poland. Avoid vague references — examiners reward specific evidence. For significance questions on the July Plot or White Rose, remember to assess both contemporary significance (immediate impact on the regime) and long-term significance (how they are remembered and what they reveal about the limits of dissent).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The German Home Front changed dramatically after Stalingrad (February 1943) — Goebbels declared 'total war', living conditions worsened, Allied bombing intensified and women were increasingly mobilised for factory work.
  • Opposition existed but was brutally suppressed: the White Rose (1942–43) distributed leaflets and its leaders were executed; the July Plot (1944) narrowly failed to kill Hitler and led to approximately 7,000 arrests and around 4,980 executions.
  • The Final Solution escalated from the Einsatzgruppen shootings (1941) to the industrialised death camps coordinated at the Wannsee Conference (January 1942). Approximately six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust. Germany surrendered unconditionally on 8 May 1945.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Wannsee Conference (January 1942).
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks awarded for a developed feature, e.g.:
• The Wannsee Conference (20 January 1942) was a meeting of senior Nazi officials that coordinated the bureaucratic machinery for the systematic murder of all European Jews — the 'Final Solution'. By involving multiple government departments, the conference ensured that the genocide was carried out as an organised state programme. [2 marks]
1 mark awarded for simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of opposition to the Nazi regime during the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Two features identified with basic description.
Secure: Each feature described with context, e.g.:
• The White Rose student group at Munich University distributed leaflets calling for passive resistance to Hitler in 1942–43. Its leaders, Hans and Sophie Scholl, were arrested in February 1943, tried before the People's Court and executed. [2 marks]
• The July Plot (20 July 1944) was an attempt by Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg and other military officers to assassinate Hitler. The bomb failed to kill Hitler; approximately 7,000 people were arrested in reprisals, and around 4,980 were executed. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the deteriorating conditions on the German Home Front after 1943.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Analyses the mechanism and its impact on civilian life.
Example: Allied bombing campaigns caused enormous damage to German cities and industrial production from 1943 onwards. The firebombing of Hamburg in July–August 1943 killed an estimated 37,000 civilians and left around one million homeless. Factories were destroyed or forced to disperse, disrupting military production. The psychological impact was equally significant — civilians could no longer feel safe in major German cities. The bombing consumed enormous German resources in anti-aircraft defences, diverting them from the military front.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the declaration of 'total war' in February 1943 for life in Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple identification.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Explores longer-term consequences and links to other developments.
Example: Goebbels' declaration of total war in February 1943 led to the full mobilisation of the German economy. Women who had previously been encouraged to stay at home were drafted into factory and agricultural work, directly contradicting the pre-war Nazi ideology of Kinder, Küche, Kirche. The regime's willingness to abandon its own social policies under military pressure demonstrated the priority it placed on survival over ideology, and also showed how war transformed German society in ways that were hard to reverse.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the July Plot (1944) for the Nazi regime.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple description.
Developing: Some assessment.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time.
Mastering: Weighs significance against other events; considers what the plot revealed about the regime.
At the time: The failure strengthened Hitler's belief in his destiny; approximately 7,000 arrests and around 4,980 executions followed; the role of the SS and Gestapo was enhanced relative to the traditional military.
Over time: Symbolically important — demonstrated that resistance existed even within the military and Nazi elite; the conspirators have been commemorated as evidence that 'another Germany' existed beneath the dictatorship.

practice_questions.text:
'Goebbels' propaganda was the most important factor in maintaining German civilian support during the Second World War.' How far do you agree?
In your answer consider other factors alongside propaganda and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Mostly descriptive, no judgement.
Developing: Some argument on both sides, limited evidence.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence; clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Weighs propaganda against other factors (economic conditions, fear of the SS/Gestapo, genuine belief in Nazism, military success) and argues a nuanced position.

For propaganda: Controlled all media; celebrated early victories; 'total war' speech in 1943 rallied support even after Stalingrad.
Against as most important: Fear of the Gestapo may have suppressed dissent rather than generating genuine support; economic policy (consumer goods, employment) was more material; military success in early years generated real enthusiasm; total war conditions from 1943 reduced genuine support despite propaganda.

What was the Wannsee Conference of January 1942?
options: A meeting to plan the invasion of the Soviet Union
A conference on wartime economic production
A rally celebrating German military victories
A meeting coordinating the systematic murder of European Jews

knowledge_checks.q: The White Rose resistance group was based at _____ University.
The July Plot assassination attempt on Hitler took place on 20 July _____.
Match each event to its correct description.
right: Student resistance group executing leaflets at Munich University
Military assassination attempt on Hitler, 20 July 1944
SS mobile killing squads operating in occupied Soviet territory
January 1942 meeting coordinating the Final Solution

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Wannsee Conference, and what was decided?
flashcard_questions.a: 20 January 1942; senior Nazis coordinated the systematic murder of European Jews — the Final Solution.

flashcard_questions.a: Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg, on 20 July 1944.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did the July Plot fail?
flashcard_questions.a: The briefcase containing the bomb was moved behind a heavy table leg, shielding Hitler from the blast.

flashcard_questions.a: Approximately 33,771 Jews were killed over two days.

30 April 1945, by suicide in his bunker beneath the Berlin Reich Chancellery.

glossary_terms.definition: Nazi Minister of Propaganda and Public Enlightenment, who controlled press, radio and film throughout the war and declared 'total war' after Stalingrad in February 1943.
SS mobile killing squads that followed German forces into occupied Soviet territory from 1941, carrying out mass shootings of Jews, Roma and Soviet officials.
A meeting of senior Nazi officials on 20 January 1942 at which the systematic murder of all European Jews — the 'Final Solution' — was coordinated.
A student resistance group at Munich University, 1942–43, whose leaders Hans and Sophie Scholl were arrested and executed for distributing anti-Nazi leaflets.
The failed assassination attempt on Hitler by Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg on 20 July 1944, followed by mass arrests and executions of conspirators.
The Nazi programme for the systematic murder of all European Jews, coordinated from 1942 and carried out primarily in death camps in occupied Poland.
The full mobilisation of a nation's economy and society for the war effort, declared by Goebbels in February 1943 following the German defeat at Stalingrad.
